subject: Post-call: latency onramp & streaming behavior (TTFT / chunking)
messages:
From: Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@edgepay.com>
To: Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwood.ai>, Camila Reyes <camila_reyes@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 9 May 2027 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Follow-up: TTFT targets and streaming strategy

Thanks for the call today — quick recap from our side and a few clarifying questions so we can align with our infra team. High-level: EdgePay is building an approvals chat that will multiplex hundreds of concurrent sessions per pod. Important constraints below.

- Target production SLOs: 95th percentile TTFT <= 220ms for short replies (avg output size ~40 tokens).
- Peak concurrency: 800 concurrent sessions per deployment region; sustained convergent QPS expected 600 rps during peak business hours.
- Throughput requirement: ability to sustain bursts up to 1.2k rps for ~2 minutes with graceful degradation.
- Streaming preference: SSE preferred (simplicity of proxies), but websocket fallback acceptable for lower-latency priming. Need guidance on chunk cadence and warmstart behavior.

Questions:
1) Do you see any obvious gaps between our targets and Redwood Dedicated baseline for the "medium-serve" instance type you mentioned?
2) How should we configure chunk cadence and heartbeat to keep TTFT at 95p while enabling long-form streaming when needed?
3) Any recommendations on KV cache warmstart or model variant pinning for predictable first-token times?

I'll attach the quick probe results from our demo VM (CSV) and the internal perf sheet from today. Appreciate an action-oriented next steps list.

--
Alex Rivera
Head of Product
EdgePay Solutions

From: Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwood.ai>

Date: Mon, 10 May 2027 09:04:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Follow-up: TTFT targets and streaming strategy

Alex — thanks for the clear summary and for sending the probe data. Short answer up front: your 95p TTFT target (<=220ms) is aggressive but achievable with the right config and a small set of mitigations.

High-level findings from quick pass on your CSV: median TTFTs in your demo look OK; the heavy tail spikes are correlated with cold KV cache and concurrent token contention. Two levers we recommend:

1) Warmstart + pinning: pin a smaller, quantized model variant for the first-token path and keep a tiny warm cache per connection (prefetch top-k prefixes for known prompts). This lowers cold-start tail.
2) Chunk cadence + heartbeat: emit an initial small chunk (8–12 tokens) immediately on first token generation, then switch to 40–80 token chunks for throughput. Use a 1s heartbeat to keep SSE connections alive across proxies.

Proposed next steps (quick mutual action plan):
- Redwood: provide an ops playbook for the pinning + warmstart pattern (deliverable: config snippet and expected perf numbers). Due: Wed 2027-05-12.
- EdgePay: share representative prompt samples and a short list of burst windows (UTC timestamps) for a 48h probe. Due: Tue 2027-05-11.
- Joint: schedule a 60-minute engineering session to run an extended probe under a controlled concurrency profile. Suggested slot: Thu 2027-05-13 10:00 PT.

Cc'ing Camila to run the ops/implementation handoff and Ben for a quick latency-run checklist.

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Follow-up: TTFT targets and streaming strategy

Looping in a few practical details after reviewing the probe CSV and our infra runbooks. TL;DR: the 8–12 token initial chunk + 40–80 follow-on chunk cadence is the right starting point for your workload. Notes:

- Initial chunk (8 tokens): keeps the first token generation path short and helps primes be emitted faster from the KV path. Use a 4–8ms inter-token pacing inside the chunk on GPU-optimized runtimes to avoid microbursts hitting the scheduler.
- Follow-on chunks (40–60 tokens): balances network overhead and token compute; if you need lower latency at the expense of slightly higher ops, drop to 20–30 tokens.
- SSE vs WebSocket: SSE is simpler through common CDNs/proxies; however, websocket has slightly lower end-to-end jitter in our tests when you need sub-150ms 95p. Since your target is 220ms, SSE + the warmstart above should be fine. Keep websocket on standby for the top 5% of traffic.
- Concurrency shaping: implement a soft-client-side token queue with a server-side admission policy. Enforce a per-connection concurrency cap (e.g., 4 in-flight requests) and a short retry/backoff for 429s. That keeps head-of-line blocking down.
- Telemetry: enable per-token timing (emit-first-token, chunk-emit, total-stream-time) and include server-side queue depth in traces. We'll provide the labeling keys in the runbook.
